style_when: the news is structural and abstract — a stack reordered, a layer added, a flow rerouted — and there is no literal object that carries it, so the idea is stated as a small physical assembly of recognisable parts rather than as bare shapes
prompt: A matte clay 3D render of an adjustable mechanical track with an expanding sliding bracket, positioned with extreme asymmetry, assembly off-centre right. The interlocking parts are constructed from matte graphite and safety yellow moulded polymer, featuring visible moulding seams and crisp mechanical edges. The structure is laid out on a weathered brushed steel console in an industrial control room. A single directional key light from the left rakes across the matte surfaces, casting long, sharp contact shadows against the metal. Bone white accents, deliberate spatial construction, no text.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, plain void background, typography, labels
rationale: A clay render distills the abstract mathematical concept of an expanding error margin into a tangible, physical assembly. It avoids literal ship clichés while perfectly capturing the systemic shift in how control towers should measure variance.
subject: an adjustable mechanical track with an expanding sliding bracket
core_thesis: Arrival-prediction error scales as a share of the remaining voyage, requiring alert windows to be dynamic percentages rather than fixed flat hours.
core_conflict: Static flat-hour alert rules versus the escalating mathematical reality of prediction error over long transit distances.

title: The Math Of ETA Prediction
